en: Diplomatic Transcript (1a1) Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now, the *Raktayamāri-tantra* is written. (1a2) Oṃ, homage to Raktayamāri. Now, King Vajradhara should contemplate the mantra for protection against being bitten by venomous creatures upon waking from sleep. (1a3) By means of the fourfold protective recitation and the collection of white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), the act of awakening one who has fallen asleep [due to poison] should be performed; he will live, of this there is no doubt. Śānta śu-

The knower of yoga should always meditate on the *klayamadya* [mudrā]; one should mutter the *siddhārtha* seeds while holding them in the hand for the sake of the fourfold protection. Having made the bitten person's face pleasant, if he has been seized by a *kāra*, he will undoubtedly rise up by means of mustard seed (*sarṣapa*) applied there. This is the meditation for the purpose of accomplishing the goal.

[Visualizing] the syllable *hūṃ*, which resembles snow, and reciting the mantra beginning with *hrīḥ ṣṭryā*, one should draw out the poison by means of light rays. Likewise, one should place an eight-petaled lotus in the right hand and the left; in its center, one should place the syllable *hūṃ*, which emits nectar through its light rays. Furthermore, the wise one should contemplate the syllable *haḥ* in the middle of a cool-rayed lunar disc upon his own head. Then, by means of the staff [of the visualization], one should draw out the poison using the mantra beginning with *hrīḥ ṣṭryā*.

(1b4) Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ haḥ hūṃ jaḥ phuḥ. With this mantra, one should wipe [the patient] with the mantras, beginning from the head down to the feet. One should visualize a rain of nectar; he will live, there is no doubt. The supreme binding of the earth, produced from the seed-syllables, should be visualized at the site of the bite as arising in yellow color. With the syllable *praṇava* (*oṃ*) at the beginning and the *visarga* at the end, the two [syllables] *ha* and *ṇa* are applied according to the rule; they effect the binding of the poison when impelled.
(2a1) [This] too is easily understood by yogins as the pacification of headaches.

(2a2) Likewise, other [afflictions] such as *lūtā*, *viṭaka*, *vicarcikā*, and so forth, are removed like diseases through the application of medical treatments for the breasts and the neck. (2a3) Then King Vajradhara, the employer of the protection wheel, [subdues] the obstacles and impediments.
(2a4) And for the sake of subduing the wicked, he said: "O Illustrious One, I am the wielder of the staff, engaged in the application of the wheel of power (*cakraprayoga*).

With my blazing body, I shall shatter those born of the three bodies (*trikāya*). O Goddess, you are the witness for all the Buddhas and Protectors. I, the master of the mandala (*maṇḍalācārya*) who slays Yama, am drawing the mandala. Having bound my face with a silken cloth (*kauśika*),"
(2b1) To those at the door of the maṇḍala house, he should say, "Who are you, sir? He should reply, "I am Subhaga.
Having drawn aside the curtain, the wise one should request the excellent guru with great devotion for the sake of initiation, uttering [the prayer] three times:
"Just as the Buddhas were consecrated by the Great Dharmas and Vajrasattva, O Lord, please consecrate me as well."

Or let them grant me whatever I desire; likewise, the disciple should respectfully present song, instrumental music, worship, water for the guest-offering, and water for washing the feet, or else have praises offered there. Then the King Vajradhara should proclaim emptiness.
1. An ornamental symbol, similar to the Tibetan *ru kha bzhi mig* (four-cornered cross) but without the two side dots.

Diplomatic transcript (3a1): *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako haṃ | oṃ pūjāvajrasvabhāvātmako haṃ || oṃ dharmadhātu-svabhāvātmako haṃ ||* (3a2) *atha homaṃ pravakṣyāmi śāntikādiprabhedataḥ | yena homena si-*

Success shall be achieved through the accomplishment of all rites: with a peaceful mind in rites of pacification (*śāntika*), with a nourishing mind in rites of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), with a longing mind in rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), and with an agitated mind in rites of killing (*māraṇa*). The shape for pacification is circular; that for enrichment is square; that called the half-moon is for subjugation; and that for killing is like the element of space (*khadhātu*). It should be one cubit in length.

It should be two cubits long for pacification (*śānti*) and likewise for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). As it is for nourishment, so it is for subduing (*śyai*) on the first lunar day (*pratipad*); however, the fire-oblation for pacification is on the full moon, while that for nourishment is on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), and the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*) is on the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*). For pacification, a rosary made of *śauktika* or *kaṭika* is recommended; pearl is highly praised. For health, conch, *putrajīva*, and *nṛpāvartaka* are used. Red sandalwood and red coral are especially excellent. Likewise, *rudrākṣa*, *hariṣṭa*, human bone, and the hood of a snake [are used].

In rites for pacification (*śāntika*), there is one hundred and one; likewise, in rites for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), eight more. In rites for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), there are twenty-five according to the distinction.
[The materials are] red sandalwood, with blood and especially coral; *rudrākṣa* seeds, *hariṣṭa*, and human bone.

Likewise for the *nāgaphaṇī* [mālā]: one hundred for *śāntika*, one hundred and eight for *pauṣṭika*, twenty-five for *vaśya* and *ākarṣaṇa*, and sixty-four for *abhicāruka*. The mantra practitioner should string together fifty beads for the accomplishment of mantras; however, for all other types of garlands, he should string them with two *merus*. For *śāntika*, it rests on the index finger; for *pauṣṭika*, on the middle finger; for *vaśya* and *ākarṣaṇa*, on the ring finger; and for [the remaining rites], on the little finger.

(4a6) For subjugation; for pacification, one should meditate on [the deity] as white in color, and for enrichment, yellow in color. For subduing, one should always meditate on [him] as red; for killing, black is considered appropriate. The Chapter on the Ritual of Fire Offering from the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittavajraraktayamāritantra*. A yogin endowed with the fourfold yoga, consuming various kinds of food and drink...

One should visualize [the mandala] as filled with perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, flags, and so forth, associated with what is to be chewed, sucked, drunk, and licked; and with musical instruments making the five great sounds. In front, one should arrange an offering (*bali*)—whether on carts, shoulder-poles, or baskets—even down to three handfuls of water sufficient for a single meal—provided with whatever is available and endowed with the *samaya* substances. Having rendered that [offering] luminous (*prabhāsvarīkṛta*), one should begin the meditation. One should visualize a lotus in the *khadhātu*.

An eight-petalled lotus with filaments; in its pericarp, by means of the syllable *yaṃ*, a wind-maṇḍala of dark-green color, shaped like a bow, with fluttering banners at both ends and marked with six white flags. Above that, from a red *ra*, arises a triangular fire-maṇḍala, red in color and marked with the syllable *ra* at its three corners. Above that, from the transformation of two *ru* syllables, are three severed heads situated upon the pericarp. Therein is a lotus vessel produced from a red *āḥ*; it is white on the outside and red in the center. One should visualize the form of an eight-petaled lotus there.

(5a5) Therein, in the eastern petal and so forth, one should visualize the syllables *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *jriṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ* as having the nature of Vairocana and the other [Tathāgatas]; and likewise in the corners beginning with the southeast, the syllables *lāṃ*, *māṃ*, *yāṃ*, *tāṃ*, and *vaṃ* as having the nature of Locanā and the other [Bodhisattvas]. These ten syllables transform into the five kinds of sacrificial offerings (*pañcāmṛta*), such as cow flesh and the rest, which are marked by these seed-syllables.

(5b3) One should visualize the substances of the pledge within that lotus vessel; above them, having meditated upon the syllable *oṃ* of white color, one should perceive the form of a stream [of nectar]. Then, one should see a moon disc born from the syllable *oṃ*, and upon that, a staff-vajra (*vajradaṇḍa*) arising from a white syllable *hūṃ*, marked with its seed-syllable. Furthermore, below that lotus vessel, in the powder, preceded by the recitation and meditation of the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* seven times, there is an uninterrupted, awakened, and abundant wind—

While meditating on the fire-mandala illuminated by a [vajra] mandala, one should visualize the ten substances of the pledge, such as cow dung and so forth—whose entire forms are ablaze with many flames—as being melted and stirred by a vajra-staff. Then, one should further contemplate that the vajra-staff itself melts into nectar, having the color of the rising sun and the appearance of quicksilver (*pārada-rasa*). Therein, having seen the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, then, by the masses of rays of light emanating from those three syllables, all...

(6b1) One should bring forth a vast abundance of nectar existing throughout the three worlds and cause it to enter right there. From that entry, (6b2) one should stabilize the form of the nectar, which is cooler than the mass of cool-rayed [moon] beams. Afterwards, one should empower it with the three syllables; endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, (6b3–6b4) having diligently produced the *bali* through the application of the nectar of gnosis, pure as the rays of the autumn moon, the mantra-practitioner, assuming the form of Yamāri, [should offer it] to the wrathful deities.

Having emanated [deities] with nooses and goads in their hands at the pillars of the directions, one should imagine [the victim] pierced by the goad, bound around the neck with the noose, and being led away. Then: *hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ* [and so forth], transformed—

*Nana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Summon the wicked Indra together with his retinue! Jaḥ!* With this mantra, together with the *prākṣa* [flower], one should bring forth Gaura, who is seated upon a white elephant and holds a vajra and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) in his right hand, and having brought him, establish him in the east.

With that same mantra, one should establish Upendra upon a Garuḍa throne, wearing a jewel crown, holding a mace and a discus in his right hands, and holding a conch and the Kaustubha gem in his left hands; [he should be placed] to the left of that very [deity], at a distance of one *nāḍī*. Furthermore, with that same [mantra], one should establish Varuṇa, white in color, riding upon a serpent, and holding a snake-noose in his hand, in the west. Furthermore, with that same—

(7b1) Or, having established Kuvera in the north—yellow in color, seated upon a treasure, with a *bījapūraka* fruit and a *nakulī* plant in his hands—one should likewise establish Śauṇḍin in the southeast, white in color, seated upon a mouse, holding a rosary and an axe in his right hands, and a radish and a sweetmeat (*modaka*) in his left. By that same [direction], one should establish Īśāna in the northeast, white in color, mounted upon a bull, bearing victory, with a trident and a skull-bowl in his hands, and embracing Gaurī with both arms. Again, by that same [direction], one should establish Agni in the southeast, seated upon a red goat, with a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his hands.
Having established [the ritual], he again [visualized] that very Rākṣasa mounted upon a corpse, holding a skull-bowl in his hand, blue in color, and full of wrath.

Having stationed the enraged [deity] in the southwest, again by that same [mantra], one should station Vāyu, smoke-colored, mounted upon a yellow lion, wearing a garment of wind, in the northwest. Again by that same [mantra], one should station Bhānu, red, holding a lotus with both hands, mounted upon seven horses, above. Again by that same [mantra], one should station Candra, white, holding a night-lotus with both hands, above. Again by that same [mantra], one should station Brahmā, fair-complexioned, four-faced.

Having positioned below [him] one who holds a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), a staff, and a rosary (*akṣa*), with his hand adorned by matted locks (*jaṭā*); and again, having positioned by that same [person] the Earth Goddess (*pṛthvīdevatā*) seated upon a lotus, holding a vase in her left hand and making the gesture of assent (*pratijñābhyupagama*) with her right hand; and again, having positioned by that same [person] the blue Vaiśravaṇa standing on a chariot, holding a sword and a threatening forefinger (*tarjanī*) in his left hands; then, having drawn forth the wrathful deities (*krodha*) in the form of Yamāntaka, holding spikes (*kīlaka*) in their hands, with the flames of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) at their hearts hanging from the necks of the wrathful ones.
NB fol. 9 is missing. Diplomatic transcript (10a1):
One should reflect upon them according to their respective locations within the eyes and so forth; having established the eyes and so forth, [one reflects] upon the body and so forth.

Having given the vajra-water and so forth, as well as the empowerment, the state of having Yamāntaka as a crown ornament, and having offered the rinsing water, the sprinkling, the sipping of water, and so on, and subsequently having first prepared the offering of the *bali* according to the sequence for accomplishing the nectar (*amṛta*),
one should consecrate it with the three truths while reciting the mantra. Then, having visualized the application of their tongues, one should [offer] the nectar.

One should offer it with this mantra: *Oṃ raktakuṭāya raktajatāya mukhāya raktaśarīrāya raktabhujāya raktamuṇḍamālābharaṇāya raktarathasamārūḍhāya raktapadmāsanāya raktābharaṇāya raktābharaṇabhūṣaṇāya! Accept this offering, accept it! Remove obstacles, remove them! Ward off the four Māras, ward them off!
Terrify, terrify! Confound, confound! Cut, cut! Pierce, pierce! Destroy, destroy!*

(10b4) *śoṣaya śoṣaya cheda cheda bheda bheda hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā* || Afterwards, one should distribute [the portions] according to their respective shares: (10b5) *oṃ indrāya namaḥ hrīḥ yamāya namaḥ ṣṭrīḥ varuṇāya namaḥ*.
(11a1) Viḥ, obeisance to Kubera; Kṛḥ, obeisance to Īśvara; Ta, obeisance to Agni; Ā, obeisance to Nairṛti.

(11a2) Not [to Vāyu]: *namaḥ* not [to Vāyu]. To Candra: *namaḥ hūṃ*. To Arka: *namaḥ hūṃ*. To Brahmā: *namaḥ bhaḥ phaṭ*. To Vasundharā: *namaḥ phaṭ*. To Vemacitrin: *namaḥ svā*. To all *bhūtas*: *namaḥ hā*. (11a4) *hī hī hī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ sphaṃ sphaṃ sphaṃ*. Afterwards, one should offer flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth. Those who are well-disposed toward the practitioner partake of the enjoyment of all tastes, flavors, and other things therein; remaining in that place—

(11b1) He should follow [the ritual], brandishing the vajra and playing the bell with graceful ease. After having informed the intended [deity] by means of Moharati and the others, at the conclusion of the satiation, he should recite the mantra of the eightfold laughter. Therein, this is the mantra: *hā hā he he ho ho hūṃ hūṃ*—one should cause [the deity] to dissolve. By means of *oṃ āḥ mur*, after that, [he should perform the dissolution] for the practitioner as well.

It is said: "The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished; success has been attained according to the [spiritual] lineage. Go to the domain of the Buddhas, and return once more! This concludes the Chapter on the Bali Offering from the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittavajraraktayamāritantra*.

Diplomatic Transcript (12a1) Then indeed, all the Blessed Tathāgatas praised the Blessed One Mahāvajrasattva: “You are the intrinsic nature of the Vajra of Delusion (*mohavajrasvabhāva*), Yamāri, most terrifying; you are the Teacher consisting of all Buddhas. Homage to you, O Kāyavajra! “You are the intrinsic nature of the Vajra of Malice (*piśunavajrasvabhāva*), Yamāri, most terrifying; you resemble the Vajra of Mind (*cittavajra*). Homage to you, O Ratnavajra! [You are] the passion...”

You are the intrinsic nature of the Cow-Vajra; homage to you, the source of the dharma of passion! You are the supreme among all faults and the foremost of the excellent; homage be to you, Vāgvajra! You are the intrinsic nature of the Envy-Vajra, Yamāri, the performer of all activities; resembling the Body-Vajra, homage be to you, Khaḍgapāṇi! You are the intrinsic nature of all Buddhas, the singular synthesis of all Buddhas; [homage to you], the excellence of all Buddhas...

(12b1) "O foremost one, Lord of the Maṇḍala, homage be to you! O Vajra-eye, Vajra-ear, Vajra-nose, Vajra-tongue, Vajra-body, Vajra-mind! Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Samaya of the Empowerment of the Vajra Eye and so forth. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the terrible maṇḍala of Yamāri, who resembles Yamāri himself and accomplishes all desired aims.
With a new, well-prepared, perfectly measured, and fresh thread, the wise one should trace the maṇḍala of Yamāntaka.

It is complete with all characteristics, the destroyer of all misfortunes, the source of pacification and other rites, a maṇḍala in the form of a maṇḍala. Therein, he should draw a five-pronged Karmavajra on all sides; in its center—
2. The *virāma* is signaled by the omission of the sūtra.
Diplomatic transcript (13a1): "One should draw a vajra crowded with vajra-flames. On the eastern prong, one should draw a vajra crowded with vajra-rays. Da-

In the eastern [direction], one should draw a jewel, filled with a garland of rays. In the west, one should draw a lotus, possessing the luster and radiance of a ruby (*padmarāga*). In the north, one should draw a sword, with a brilliance equal to the color of a cloud. In the eastern corner, one should draw a wheel; in the south, one should draw a vajra; in the west, one should draw a lotus with its bud fully blossomed; and in the north—

One should draw a sword filled with five-colored rays. At the eastern gate, a mallet; at the southern, a vajra-staff; at the western gate, a lotus; and at the northern, a sword-vajra. Having recognized that the maṇḍala is completed, one should perform the worship.

(13b1) Specifically, one should worship the Buddhas with the five objects of sensual pleasure, free from hesitation. In the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittavajraraktayamāritantra*, this is the chapter on the Great Maṇḍala. Then, indeed, the Blessed Ones, all the Blessed Tathāgatas, requested the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, Mahāvajradhara, with many kings of hymns: "Please explain the application of the mudrās by which the Vajra-holders are pleased; when sealed with the Vajra-mudrā, they bring about abundant accomplishment. Then King Vajradhara uttered these words: "One should visualize Yamaghna upon the heads of all those belonging to the maṇḍala. One should constantly draw the maṇḍala; constantly [perform] the homa..."

One should worship with the diplomatic transcript (14a1); one should always accomplish the commitments (*samaya*) and then cause [the disciple] to take up the vows (*saṃvara*). First, with one [mantra], [one should bestow] the crown; second, one should take up the sword; third, the vajra-bell; and fourth, the consumption of the moon (14a3). These four great consecrations (*mahāseka*) should be emitted from the mouth of the Red One. By the power of these consecrations, the supreme Victors attained awakening (14a4). Now I shall proclaim the mantra for the ritual of the offering to all spirits (*sarvabhūtabali*): *uccā-*...

(14a5) Apart from the great mantra that causes all spirits to tremble—the seed-syllables of the mantra beginning with *hrīḥ* and *ṣṭryā*, joined with *svāhā* at the end—having prepared three mandalas mixed with feces, urine, and water, the yogin should gratify the deity. He should then recollect the sound of "hā hā. Having prepared the three mandalas, [measuring] eight or twelve [units].

(14b2) Having drawn sixteen [squares] according to the rule, the wise one should place the mantras everywhere. The practitioner should place the perfected mantras in the twelfth cell. The three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, will be accomplished without exception or remainder: YA MA RĀ JĀ SA DO ME YA YA ME DĀ RUṆA YO DA YA YA DA YO.

*Nirayākṣe ya*, *yakṣaya cca nirāmayā*. One should first place *ya* in the center; in the south, the *maṃjuvajraka*; having written the letter *ma* in the west, one places the tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*) in the north. Taking the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*)...
[end of diplomatic transcript]

One who maintains [this] in the direction of emptiness (*śūnya*), having interlaced it with two *hūṃ*s, shall accomplish all tasks. And as for "ni rā jā sa ho ru ṇa yo ni ra" and so forth on the exterior: having inscribed it starting from the left, this is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for all purposes. It should be written in the single isolated square in front of the third enclosure. Starting from the east, with the mantras beginning with *hrīḥ ṣṭrī* and so forth, one should likewise write them in the eight squares immediately following that. [The effects are: "Make mute," "Kill," "Expel," "Subjugate," "Cause enmity," "Perform pacification (*śānti*)," "Perform nourishment (*puṣṭi*)," and so on.

(15a6) These [mantras] are according to the [specific] action; they begin with *Oṃ* and end with *Namaḥ*, and at the end are made to have *Vaṣaṭ*, *Voṣaṭ*, *Hūṃ*, and *Phaṭ*. These seed-syllables effect pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśa*), and destruction (*anta*). In the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittavajraraktayamāritantra*, this is the chapter on consecration named "The Surveying of the Wheel. The world is overcome by hatred...

Having seen the world overcome by hatred, the Blessed One, out of compassion, assumed the true form of Mahāyamāri, the destroyer of all hatred. Having seen the world overcome by delusion, the Blessed One, out of compassion, assumed the true form of Mohayamāri, the destroyer of all delusion. Having seen the world overcome by malice, the Blessed One, out of compassion, assumed the true form of Piśunayamāri, the destroyer of all malice.

(16a1) Out of compassion, the Blessed One performed this: seeing the world overcome by passion, he who brings about the destruction of all passion created, out of compassion, the Blessed One in the form of Rāgayamāri. Seeing the world overcome by envy, he who brings about the destruction of all envy created, out of compassion, the Blessed One in the form of Īrṣyāyamāri. Maitrī is said to be Carcikā, and Karuṇā is likewise Vārāhī; Muditā is to be known as Sarasvatī, and Upekṣā has the form of Gaurī. By means of the self, all—

Having brought all phenomena to completion as the maṇḍala, the yogin should emanate [them] from the seed-syllable; he will attain accomplishment, of this there is no doubt. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme characteristic of conduct, [the practice] of Yamāribhīma.

For the accomplishment of body, speech, and mind through form, in regions of great forests, having mounted a supreme buffalo and having made ornaments of snakes, one should meditate upon the iron vajra. One’s hair should be made tawny and especially standing upright; having wrapped it around the head-hair, one should make the beard tawny. [The mantra] *hrīḥ ṣṭryādi*...

Having brandished the vajra-staff, one should then let out a lion’s roar through the application of the Raktayamāri ritual. Having encountered some common person, one should enter the city with distress. One should cause a beautiful song to be sung, such as the *ṣāḍava* and other melodies. Then, having seen a banner and a street, one should prepare milk there. [Milk...
Diplomatic transcript.

With a mind focused through practice, one should accomplish Mahāmudrā; having assumed the form of Vārāhī, all women tremble. The yogin should roam like a lion, accomplishing all desired aims. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the accomplishment of Śatavāha; one should prescribe the recitation of his single-syllable great mantra. One should visualize [him] as having the face of a buffalo, born from the seed-syllable *ṣṭrī*, mounted upon a buffalo in a vajra-maṇḍala.

One should contemplate: whatever various weapons exist upon the earth, the wise one should visualize them as the arms of the Sadhana of Mahiṣānana. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Sadhana of Vajradaṇḍa—the great mantra consisting of the syllable Hrīḥ, whose vehicle is a great buffalo, who possesses two hundred thousand arms, whose body is smeared with ashes, and who, towering like Mount Sumeru, treads upon the depths of the netherworld (rasātala). Now, therefore—

(17b3) I shall fully proclaim the accomplishment of Koṭibāhu, the great mantra of Vikṛtānana, which arises from the syllable *hūṃ*, [performed by] the Lord: *oṃ vikṛtānana hūṃ hā hāḥ hīḥ hūṃ hūṃ heḥ haiḥ hoḥ haḥ svāhā*.

(17b5) Therefore, I shall explain the accomplishment of the pledge (*samayasādhana*) for the sake of the successful fulfillment of all activities. For one who is exhausted by mantras, the food offering (*nivedya*) is extremely difficult to obtain: namely, the great flesh of the horse and especially that of the elephant; as well as the form of a cow and a dog. [kha] Diplomatic transcript.

(18a1) And likewise for a kingdom and a pack of jackals. Having anointed [the body] with great oil mixed with *nilī*, one should cook it. By the mere act of this anointing, one brings the entire world under control. (18a2) [One should take] *rocanā*, *sinduvāra*, and likewise the *bilva* mantra; together with half a measure of powdered *iṣṭāka*, or with the juice of gold leaves—having smeared the body with this, one should drink the great [elixir]. (18a3) [The practitioner] should drink it.

Likewise, there is the Vajrāmṛta. This is the most excellent and supreme yoga, like the drinking of the Svayambhū flower. The Chapter on the Practice of the Samaya and the Means of Achievement from the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittavajraraktayamāri-tantra*.

(18a6) Then the Blessed One, having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in the form of Mahāpuruṣasamaya, having entered the meditative absorption in the form of Vajravārāhī, having entered the meditative absorption in the form of Sarasvatī, and having entered the meditative absorption in the form of Gaurī, uttered this song of worship: "Aḍeḍe! One should place [the offerings]. One should arrange flowers, incense, lamps, and fragrant perfumes in the directions beginning with the southeast. For one who possesses the yoga of Vajrapātāla, a fissure arises in a dream. Now, therefore, it is proclaimed—

I shall describe the mandala of the King of Horses for the sake of accomplishing the state of moving through the sky. One should propitiate the Supreme Horse (Paramāśva), who has two arms and one face, is dark-green in color, and is terrifying. He is mounted upon the sun, has the face of a horse, and is most fearsome. In his right hand he holds a fist at his nose, and in his left hand a skull-cup. The wise practitioner should recite this mantra—*oṃ phūṃ phūṃ hrīḥ hrīḥ*—for the sake of accomplishing the Supreme Horse. One should meditate on Vajravīṇā in the east, Turaṅgamā in the south, Saptirāja in the west, and Paramāśvā in the north. [He is] the Lord.

One should meditate upon all [the goddesses] with both arms crossed; by this mantra, the ritual dismissal (*utsarga*) of all of them is thus proclaimed. Likewise, there is a pure mark on the right, just as the mantra of the Supreme Horse is sharp like the Vajra-Pātālaka. Through the yoga of the meditation on the Supreme Horse, the three realms of existence are completely pervaded. [This is] the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.

With *nīnī* and *kāya*, as well as with *kṛṣṇaka* and *ajjalaka*, one makes [the color] brown; with *tālaka* alone it becomes yellowish-brown (*kapila*), and likewise with *hiṅgulaka* it becomes red.

Melted by a mind of compassionate passion, Vajradhṛk himself— One should first cultivate the yoga, the *anuyoga* as the second, the *atiyoga* as the third, and the *mahāyoga* as the fourth. The yoga of the accomplishment of all Vajrasattvas is what one should consecrate. The arising from that [accomplishment] is the deity; through application, it is the *anuyoga*. The empowerment of the wheel and so forth, as well as body, speech, and mind; the entry into the wheel of gnosis, and likewise the tasting of the nectar; the great worship, the praise, and the great yoga—these are desired for us. The master is not to be disparaged.

(33b2) One must not transgress the command of the Sugata. Likewise, out of anger, one must never disclose the faults of one’s brothers. One must not revile one’s own aggregates (*skandha*), nor should one defame the Dharma of the Blessed One. A corrupt form of loving-kindness must always be abandoned. [The Dharma... One must never disregard [the teachings]; one must certainly not deceive a faithful being. One should always observe the commitments (*samaya*). There is indeed fault in disparaging women, whose very nature is wisdom (*prajñā*). The yogi should never wander for alms, nor should he ever abandon yoga. He should always and constantly recite the mantra while constantly observing the commitments and so forth. If, however, an offense against the guru or a transgression of the commitments occurs through negligence, then one should indeed perform the mandala ritual and confess the fault to the Sugatas. One should always honor that person who is firm, a teacher who observes the commitments (*samaya*), free from anger, blinded by compassion, whose mind is devoid of all faults, who is absorbed in meditation, and devoted to the recitation of mantras. O wise one, having praised that disciple as being worthy of the status of a teacher—steadfast, disciplined, single-minded in compassion, possessing faith, commitment, and patience, devoted to Yama’s enemy [the Buddha], and devoted to the teacher—one should bring him to full maturity. Then, the Blessed Ones, the forms of supreme great bliss of all the Tathāgatas, the Vajra...

Having heard the words of the being and having attained a state of vision, they uttered this: "The ultimate tantras of the Noble Ones, the great vow ending with the skull; the tantras ending with the *samaya*—such have never existed before, nor will they exist in the future.
Alas! O Dharma, you who are profoundly peaceful yet most cruel and terrifying!"

Diplomatic transcript (35a1) Oh, the continuity of saṃsāra! Oh, how truly astonishing is this! That which is a fault would become a virtue. There is no awakening (*bodhi*), nor is there realization (*abhisamaya*); there is no entity (*bhāva*), nor is there cultivation (*bhāvanā*). There is no element (*dhātu*), nor is there consciousness (*vijñāna*); it is equal to space.

(35a3) That which is selfless like space is this great bliss of phenomena (*dharmamahāsukha*). It is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor the *kutāsana* posture. By means of the application of the *sattva*, that which is established is the Vajra. All entities are indeed not real, being devoid of beginning, middle, and end. Then, the Blessed One, Mahācañcikā, and the others uttered this inspired utterance:

(35b1) They were stainless, pure, and supremely blissful; there was a connection with the forest of merit. Compassion dwells in the mind; it is a single great treasure-mine, the very essence of compassion. (35b2–3) O Supreme Bliss, you who are beyond nature, whose essence is great happiness, whose nature is Dharma—neither full nor deficient, for what is spoken is indeed without decrease.

(35b4) Bhāu || || In the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittaraktayamāritantra*, this is the chapter on the proclamation of awakening. One who desires the state of entering the city of others, having attained the path of coming and going, should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind. Success shall be achieved by reciting it ten million times;

what need is there to mention five times ten million? Then, beginning with the initial yoga, one should, during the first stage of practice, visualize oneself as being like space and fix the mind upon a wall, so that the mind—composed of dream—goes and returns again.

In that very same way, one should act toward one's own self, yet the movement of others is their coming and going. Just as the mind travels far away, one turns it back again in an instant. Likewise, through the yoga of uninterrupted practice, one is released from the place [of distraction]. Just as an arrow, having been fixed upon a target, is released from the bowstring, so too this archer of the mind proceeds without interruption. One should settle the mind upon the moon, the conjunction of the sun, or the wind; there the mind comes and goes, its activity being thus directed.
Having taken up some heat and reached the state of a single destination, he goes to another body, just as [the sun] in summer—

Furthermore, one should understand the movement and consumption of the moon and sun through the conjunction with Rāhu. Having accomplished the station of the transits (*saṃkrānti*) by means of yoga, and having known the measure of misfortune (*ariṣṭi*), the one who characterizes the procedure for the transits brings forth the entire universe, including the moving and the unmoving, at will according to his desire. Having emitted the *apāna* as far as the anus and the genitals, one should begin it well from the navel; the *prāṇa* reaching the heart and throat should emerge from the aperture of the breath. The chapter on entering the bodies of others in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittaraktayamāritantra* is completed. May there be auspiciousness! 12.
